title: What is wholly yours
hookLine: they can't admire your cleverness, so show what's fully yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance (Meditations 5.5)

cards: Plenty of people have a sentence that starts, I'm just not. Not a math person. Not good at small talk.
Not creative. Sometimes it's true, and sometimes it's a door we've closed so we don't have to try. A Roman emperor had one too.
In his private notebook, the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius admits he isn't especially quick. Then, in book five, entry five, he turns that into a challenge.

teach.b: People can't admire your sharpness of mind, Marcus tells himself. Fine. Whether he was being modest or honest, we can't know, but he takes it as given.
Then the turn: there are many other things where you can't claim, I'm not built for that.

teach.h: SHOW WHAT'S ENTIRELY IN YOUR POWER.
teach.b: So show those, the ones entirely in your power: sincerity, dignity, endurance in hard work, not chasing pleasure, being content with what you have and with little, kindness, frankness, not loving excess, not chattering, a generous spirit.
Not one of them needs talent.
Do you see, he asks, how many of these you could show right now, with no excuse of being naturally unable? And yet you stay below the mark, by choice.

Are you forced by your nature to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your body, to try to please people, to show off, to be restless in your mind? No. You could have been free of these long ago.

teach.h: IF SLOW, WORK AT THAT TOO.
teach.b: And if you really are slower than others, he says, work at that too, and don't neglect it or enjoy being dull.
Here's what makes this kind. Nothing on Marcus's list depends on gifts. A slow thinker can be sincere.
A shy person can be kind. A tired person can refuse to grumble. Those are wholly yours.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes take one quality from the list in Meditations 5.5, such as sincerity, dignity or endurance, and practice it for a day.

o: a Roman orator well-known for his quick and brilliant mind
the emperor who believed only the gifted can be good
the emperor who said sincerity and kindness need no talent

games.q: what is mine — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus thought of himself as brilliant
in 5.5 he takes it as given that people can't admire his sharpness.
Marcus's list of qualities in 5.5 needs no special talent
sincerity, dignity, endurance, kindness: all in your power.
Marcus says slow people should give up on improving
if you're slow, he says, work at that too.

games.q: at a party you feel dull next to a witty friend. what fits Meditations 5.5?
o: be sincere and kind, which is wholly yours.
games.why: Marcus says that where cleverness isn't admired, show what's entirely in your power: sincerity, kindness, a generous spirit.

practice: Hear three of Marcus's words slowly, sincerity, dignity, endurance, and let each land for a breath. Then pick one, and picture a moment where it fits: saying what you mean, not gossiping, or finishing a hard task without complaint.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who listed what's wholly in your power even without brilliance: sincerity, dignity, endurance, kindness. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'sharpness, keenness': the quality Marcus says people can't admire in him (5.5).

carryVoice: Your line: what is mine. No talent is needed for any of it. Five hundred sixty-five days now.
